titleStmt.title: Sex differences in learning processes of classical and operant conditioning
titleStmt.author: Christina Dalla
Tracey J. Shors

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Sex differences in learning processes of classical and operant conditioning

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: sex differences in classical and operant conditioning in laboratory rodents
span.quote: In general, females perform better than males in the classical eyeblink conditioning, in fear-potentiated startle and in most operant conditioning tasks, such as the active avoidance test. However, in the classical fear conditioning paradigm, in certain lever-pressing paradigms and in the conditioned taste aversion males outperform females or are more resistant to extinction.

span.label: where sex differences appear across conditioning paradigms, and whether they reflect learning or performance
span.quote: Critically, sex differences in performance account for some of the reported effects on learning and these are discussed throughout the review.

span.label: collects sex differences across four conditioning paradigms, shows the direction depends on the task, separates organizational from activational hormonal causes, and argues females must be included in basic research
span.quote: Minimally, the presentation of sex differences in learning underscores the need to include females in basic research studies [ 30 ]. They are often not included either because of the problems inherent to monitoring the estrous cycle, but also because it is assumed that their behaviours will be similar to males, albeit more variable.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Sex differences have been reported during acquisition, retention and extinction in most of these paradigms.

span.label: sex differences in classical and operant conditioning
span.quote: We focus on classical and operant conditioning paradigms, including classical eyeblink conditioning, fear conditioning, active avoidance and conditioned taste aversion.

span.label: review
span.quote: We review here sex differences as they occur in laboratory rodent species.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The amount of fear generated by the task determines which sex performs better: high-fear paradigms favour males, low-fear paradigms favour females
span.quote: These effects seem to depend on the amount of fear that is generated and expressed during the learning experience

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Males acquire and retain the conditioned fear more strongly, and this stronger fear is what drives their superior performance in fear conditioning
span.note: status: the paper's own words: It is possible that
span.quote: It is possible that males perform better than females, because they acquire and retain the conditioned fear in a higher degree.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Divergent coping strategies to shock — active responding in females versus passive behavioural inhibition and freezing in males — produce the operant-conditioning sex difference
span.quote: Female rats respond actively to aversive stimulation, such as the footshock, whereas male rats exhibit behavioural inhibition by reacting passively and freeze

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Adult testosterone acts anxiolytically and thereby pushes males toward the passive strategy that impairs their avoidance learning
span.quote: Testosterone has been proposed to have anxiolytic properties and this might contribute to the passive strategy that male rats choose in response to the footshock

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Dendritic spine density on CA1 pyramidal cells tracks learned-response performance across hormonal and stress manipulations, and is proposed as the anatomical substrate of the sex difference
span.quote: Thus, under all these various circumstances, performance of the learned response relates in a positive way to the presence of dendritic spines in the CA1 area of the hippocampus

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Gonadal hormones act twice — organizing the developing brain and then activating circuits in puberty and adulthood — and the two effects interact to produce adult sex differences
span.quote: Thus, sex differences in learning are influenced by both organizational and activational effects of sex hormones, but in a complex and probably interactive way.

span.label: most differences are organized by gonadal hormones during early development and then modulated by activational effects in adulthood
span.quote: Most sex differences in conditioning are dependent on organizational effects of gonadal hormones during early development of the brain, in addition to modulation by activational effects during puberty and adulthood.

span.label: masculinising a female neonatally is not sufficient; male-like avoidance appears only if testosterone is also given in adulthood
span.quote: When females are masculinized by exposure to testosterone on the day of their birth, they do not perform like males as adults [ 84 , 87 ]. However, if they are also treated with testosterone in adulthood, then they exhibit male-like escape avoidance latencies

span.label: different tasks recruit different hormones - testosterone dominates avoidance, oestrogens and progesterone dominate eyeblink and fear conditioning - because the tasks differ in whether the response is volitional
span.quote: It seems that in active avoidance tasks testosterone plays a more important role than estrogens in the emergence of sex differences, while in eyeblink and fear conditioning estrogens and progesterone in females seem to be more important. These tasks differ in the fact that during operant conditioning, the animal must emit a voluntary motor response in order to learn the contingency, whereas during classical (i.e. Pavlovian) conditioning, the animal emits an obligatory unconditioned response to the unconditioned stimulus, irrespective of volition. Thus, the two types of training procedures are vastly different in terms of their dependence on volitional activity and the learning processes involved. Therefore, different hormonal factors seem to mediate each task.

span.label: the sex difference survives across the oestrous cycle, so it is not simply an oestrogen effect
span.quote: However, the sex difference is apparent even in females that are trained during diestrus, a phase of the estrous cycle characterized by lower levels of estrogens and progesterone ( Figure 1b ) [ 47 ]. Thus, sex differences are evident across the estrous cycle and are not solely dependent on the presence of estrogens in females.

span.label: an a priori argument that learning cannot depend heavily on hormone level, since both sexes undergo large hormonal changes across life
span.quote: It is noted that one would not expect a total dependence of basic learning processes on one or even a few hormones, because the adaptive value of learning is too great. Males and females of all species undergo massive changes in sex hormone availability across their lifespan, so learning cannot be massively influenced by their levels.

span.label: oestrogen dose effects are non-monotonic: low doses disrupt and high doses facilitate active avoidance
span.quote: Studies with exogenous estrogens administration showed that low doses of estrogens disrupt, while high doses facilitate acquisition of the active avoidance behaviour

span.label: The neural substrate of the reviewed sex differences is not established; hippocampal CA1 spine density is offered only as a parallel correlate.
span.note: what this limits: any claim about the neural basis of the reviewed sex differences: THE NEUROANATOMICAL SUBSTRATES THAT MIGHT ACCOUNT FOR SEX DIFFERENCES HAVE NOT BEEN IDENTIFIED
span.quote: The neuroanatomical substrates that might account for sex differences have not been identified

span.label: Performance factors can never be entirely excluded even in the eyeblink paradigm the authors regard as least contaminated by them.
span.note: what this limits: even the eyeblink evidence the review treats as cleanest: ONE CAN NEVER RULE OUT PERFORMANCE EFFECTS ENTIRELY
span.quote: That said, one can never rule out performance effects entirely.

span.label: Sex differences in spatial learning are excluded from the review's scope.
span.note: what this limits: spatial learning, which the review excludes: SEX DIFFERENCES IN SPATIAL LEARNING, ALTHOUGH IMPORTANT, WILL NOT BE DISCUSSED IN THIS REVIEW, BECAUSE THEY HAVE BEEN REVIEWED ELSEWHERE
span.quote: Sex differences in spatial learning, although important, will not be discussed in this review, because they have been reviewed elsewhere

span.label: Developmental hormone effects on conditioned taste aversion are absent from the literature reviewed.
span.note: what this limits: developmental effects of sex hormones, on which the literature is silent: TO OUR KNOWLEDGE, THERE IS NO REPORT IN THE LITERATURE CONCERNING DEVELOPMENTAL EFFECTS OF SEX HORMONES
span.quote: To our knowledge, there is no report in the literature concerning developmental effects of sex hormones.

span.label: Conditioned taste aversion is confounded by sex differences in sweet preference and in the rewarding/aversive properties of the compounds used, making learning-level conclusions hard to draw.
span.note: what this limits: the conditioned taste aversion paradigm: IT IS DIFFICULT TO STUDY SEX DIFFERENCES IN CONDITIONED LEARNING IN THIS PARADIGM, ALTHOUGH THEY EXIST
span.quote: As a result, it is difficult to study sex differences in conditioned learning in this paradigm, although they exist.

span.label: Findings on retention and extinction of cue fear conditioning are inconsistent across studies.
span.note: what this limits: the retention and extinction phases of cue fear conditioning, in a changed context, measured by freezing: WHETHER SEX DIFFERENCES EXIST DURING TESTING (RETENTION) AND EXTINCTION OF CUE FEAR CONDITIONING, WHEN RATS ARE PLACED IN A DIFFERENT CONTEXT (CR: TIME SPEND FREEZING)
span.quote: However, conflicting results have been obtained on whether sex differences exist during testing (retention) and extinction of cue fear conditioning, when rats are placed in a different context (CR: time spend freezing)

span.label: sex differences in performance account for some of the reported learning effects, a confound running through the whole literature
span.note: what this limits: every learning effect the review reports: SEX DIFFERENCES IN PERFORMANCE ACCOUNT FOR SOME OF THE REPORTED EFFECTS ON LEARNING
span.quote: Critically, sex differences in performance account for some of the reported effects on learning and these are discussed throughout the review.

span.label: some differences may be differences in strategy rather than in learning
span.note: what this limits: spatial learning paradigms specifically: THIS HAS BEEN SUGGESTED BEFORE FOR SPATIAL LEARNING PARADIGMS, IN WHICH MALE RATS USUALLY PERFORM BETTER THAN FEMALES BY USING A MORE DIRECT strategy - a strategy difference, not a learning difference
span.quote: Also, some sex differences probably do not reflect sex differences in learning, but rather sex differences in strategies. This has been suggested before for spatial learning paradigms, in which male rats usually perform better than females by using a more direct strategy

span.label: lever-pressing differences are attributable to general activity and to what females do instead of pressing
span.note: what this limits: lever-pressing measures: SEX DIFFERENCES IN LEVER-PRESSING HAVE BEEN ATTRIBUTED TO HIGHER GENERAL ACTIVITY OF FEMALES THAN MALES AND TO THE FACT THAT DURING TESTING FEMALES ENGAGE TO DIFFERENT ACTIVITIES THAN PRESSING THE LEVER
span.quote: Sex differences in lever-pressing have been attributed to higher general activity of females than males and to the fact that during testing females engage to different activities than pressing the lever

span.label: conditioned taste aversion is declared difficult to interpret for this question because taste preference, drug reward and the hormones themselves all confound it
span.note: what this limits: conditioned taste aversion studies that administer hormones: EXOGENOUS SEX HORMONE'S ADMINISTRATION ALSO HAS ILLNESS-INDUCING PROPERTIES, WHICH CAN IN TURN INFLUENCE CONDITIONED TASTE AVERSION
span.quote: To make the issue more complicated, exogenous sex hormone's administration also has illness-inducing properties, which can in turn influence conditioned taste aversion [ 121 ]. As a result, it is difficult to study sex differences in conditioned learning in this paradigm, although they exist.

span.label: drug-based aversion data cannot be evaluated from a learning perspective because of the rewarding properties of the drugs
span.note: what this limits: drug-of-abuse aversion data read as learning: IT IS DIFFICULT TO EVALUATE THEM FROM A LEARNING PERSPECTIVE, BECAUSE OF THE POTENT REWARDING PROPERTIES OF THE DIFFERENT CLASSES OF DRUGS OF ABUSE
span.quote: Although these data are very interesting, it is difficult to evaluate them from a learning perspective, because of the potent rewarding properties of the different classes of drugs of abuse.

span.label: human sex differences are small, task-dependent and hard to interpret even when observed
span.note: what this limits: human cognition studies: MANY OF THE REPORTED SEX DIFFERENCES ARE RELATIVELY SMALL IN MAGNITUDE AND THEIR EMERGENCE MAY ONLY ARISE AS A FUNCTION OF THE TASK, ITS DIFFICULTY OR THE SPECIFIC EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
span.quote: That said, many of the reported sex differences are relatively small in magnitude and their emergence may only arise as a function of the task, its difficulty or the specific experimental design [ 14 ]. For these reasons, sex differences in human cognition are difficult to be observed and once observed, even more difficult to interpret.

span.label: spatial learning is excluded from the review despite being central to the topic
span.note: duplicate of: limitations[2] · what this limits: the same scope as item 2 - spatial learning, excluded from the review
span.quote: Sex differences in spatial learning, although important, will not be discussed in this review, because they have been reviewed elsewhere

span.label: no study exists on developmental hormone effects in conditioned taste aversion
span.note: what this limits: developmental hormone work in conditioned taste aversion: THERE IS NO REPORT IN THE LITERATURE CONCERNING DEVELOPMENTAL EFFECTS OF SEX HORMONES, and SUCH STUDIES WOULD BE DIFFICULT TO DO, ALTHOUGH NOT IMPOSSIBLE
span.quote: To our knowledge, there is no report in the literature concerning developmental effects of sex hormones. Given the time course, such studies would be difficult to do, although not impossible.

span.label: the verbal-versus-spatial pattern of human sex differences, used to motivate the rodent work
span.quote: For example, women tend to outperform men on tasks that involve verbal or semantic rules and memories related to personal experience, whereas men perform better on tasks that require the manipulation of complex spatial information, such as the manipulation of shapes in space

span.label: the sex-skewed prevalence of specific disorders, used as the applied justification for the whole review
span.quote: For example, alcoholism, autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are much more common in men, whereas Alzheimer's disease, social phobias, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and major depression are more common in women

span.label: a sex difference in this literature is a difference in measured PERFORMANCE, and the review's central caution is that performance and learning are not the same thing
span.quote: Critically, sex differences in performance account for some of the reported effects on learning and these are discussed throughout the review.

span.label: organizational versus activational is the distinction between hormones building the difference during development and hormones modulating it in adulthood - and the two can be separated experimentally by when the manipulation is done
span.quote: Most sex differences in conditioning are dependent on organizational effects of gonadal hormones during early development of the brain, in addition to modulation by activational effects during puberty and adulthood.

span.label: the DIRECTION of the sex difference is not a property of sex but of the task: females lead in eyeblink, fear-potentiated startle and active avoidance, males in fear conditioning, simple lever-pressing and taste aversion
span.quote: In general, females perform better than males in the classical eyeblink conditioning, in fear-potentiated startle and in most operant conditioning tasks, such as the active avoidance test. However, in the classical fear conditioning paradigm, in certain lever-pressing paradigms and in the conditioned taste aversion males outperform females or are more resistant to extinction.

span.label: difficulty flips the direction within one paradigm - males lead on simple lever-pressing, females on the harder low-rate variant
span.quote: Thus, sex differences exist in lever-pressing paradigms with males outperforming females in simple tasks, while females performing better in more difficult tasks, such as the differential reinforcement of low rate responding.

span.label: claim_type: critique
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: existence — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Minimally, the presentation of sex differences in learning underscores the need to include females in basic research studies [ 30 ]. They are often not included either because of the problems inherent to monitoring the estrous cycle, but also because it is assumed that their behaviours will be similar to males, albeit more variable.

span.label: method: narrative review across eyeblink conditioning, fear conditioning, active avoidance and conditioned taste aversion, with hormonal manipulation studies
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: review — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Most sex differences in conditioning are dependent on organizational effects of gonadal hormones during early development of the brain, in addition to modulation by activational effects during puberty and adulthood.

span.label: phenomenon: sex differences in associative learning
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: sex differences in classical and operant conditioning — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: In general, females perform better than males in the classical eyeblink conditioning, in fear-potentiated startle and in most operant conditioning tasks, such as the active avoidance test. However, in the classical fear conditioning paradigm, in certain lever-pressing paradigms and in the conditioned taste aversion males outperform females or are more resistant to extinction.

span.label: critiques → the practice of excluding females from basic research, and the assumption that their behaviour is like males but more variable
span.quote: Minimally, the presentation of sex differences in learning underscores the need to include females in basic research studies [ 30 ]. They are often not included either because of the problems inherent to monitoring the estrous cycle, but also because it is assumed that their behaviours will be similar to males, albeit more variable.

span.label: contradicts → the assumption that females are the more variable sex, citing human data showing the opposite
span.quote: Oddly enough, in human studies, men tend to express more variance on test scores of cognitive and intellectual performance

span.label: qualifies → reported sex differences in learning, by attributing some to performance and some to strategy
span.quote: Also, some sex differences probably do not reflect sex differences in learning, but rather sex differences in strategies. This has been suggested before for spatial learning paradigms, in which male rats usually perform better than females by using a more direct strategy

span.label: supports → the case for including sex as a variable when animal models are applied to sex-differentiated disorders
span.quote: Because so many mental disorders are more prevalent on one sex than the other, it is important to consider sex differences in learning when applying animal models of learning for these disorders.

span.label: performance —causes→ sex differences
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — the review's central caution: some reported LEARNING differences are performance differences. an edge saying sex causes learning difference would carry the literature's error
span.quote: Critically, sex differences in performance account for some of the reported effects on learning and these are discussed throughout the review.

span.label: organizational —contrasted-with→ activational
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Most sex differences in conditioning are dependent on organizational effects of gonadal hormones during early development of the brain, in addition to modulation by activational effects during puberty and adulthood.

span.label: trace conditioning —contrasted-with→ delay conditioning
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS THE TRACE INTERVAL, AND IT IS GIVEN AS A NUMBER. 'This task DEPENDS ON THE HIPPOCAMPUS and REQUIRES MULTIPLE TRIALS to learn BECAUSE THE CS IS SEPARATED WITH THE US WITH A TRACE INTERVAL OF 500 MS.' The two procedures are identical except for a gap, and the sentence states the gap AS THE CAUSE of both the hippocampal dependence and the slower learning - so the axis is not a description of the difference, it is the explanation of the consequences. Q-471. · strength of the relation: 1 — separated by whether the hippocampus is required, which is what makes the pair diagnostic
span.quote: For many of our studies, we rely on a procedure known as trace conditioning. This task depends on the hippocampus and requires multiple trials to learn because the CS is separated with the US with a trace interval of 500 ms. We also observe sex differences during delay conditioning. Delay conditioning is much easier to learn than trace conditioning, because the CS and the US overlap in time; learning this association does not depend on the hippocampus

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · sex differences —operationalised-as→ eyeblink conditioning
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named only the paradigm. This sentence names both and states the paradigm as the one in which the phenomenon is examined - 'evidence for SEX DIFFERENCES in classical and operant conditioning paradigms, WITH A FOCUS ON classical EYEBLINK CONDITIONING'. — strength of the relation: 0.8 — chosen as the cleanest measure BECAUSE it is least influenced by performance factors - and even so, the review says performance effects can never be ruled out entirely
span.quote: Importantly, classical eyeblink conditioning is less influenced by performance factors that can inadvertently affect learning. That said, one can never rule out performance effects entirely.

span.label: learned helplessness —operationalised-as→ active avoidance
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: When male rats are exposed to uncontrollable stress, they do not learn to escape the shock in the active avoidance task and thus they become helpless. On the contrary, females exposed to the same regime of uncontrollable stress learn to escape and thus they do not express learned helplessness behaviour

span.label: sex differences —operationalised-as→ eyeblink conditioning
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — RE-GROUNDS dalla2009-sex-differences-in-learning-proces[3]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: In this review, we present evidence for sex differences in classical and operant conditioning paradigms, with a focus on classical eyeblink conditioning, fear conditioning, escape and active avoidance, and conditioned taste aversion.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: b. Intact females emit more conditioned responses than intact males during trace eyeblink conditioning (p<0.05).

span.label: statistical significance test
span.quote: significant differences are noted with an *

span.label: Female rats emit more conditioned eyeblink responses than males in both the hippocampus-dependent trace version and the hippocampus-independent delay version of the task.
span.quote: During both trace and delay conditioning, females outperform males

span.label: The direction of the sex difference reverses in fear conditioning: males acquire and express conditioned fear better than females.
span.quote: Thus, in general, males outperform females in fear conditioning paradigms.

span.label: On the harder two-way active avoidance task females learn to escape within the first trials while males need many more, and some males never learn at all.
span.quote: Although the task is more difficult, most females readily learn to escape the stimulus on the first trials of testing, whereas males require more trials.

span.label: Removing the ovaries in adulthood abolishes the female advantage in eyeblink conditioning, showing the effect depends on circulating ovarian hormones.
span.quote: Also, removal of ovarian hormones prevents the sex difference in performance

span.label: The sex difference in eyeblink conditioning is absent before and during puberty and only appears in adulthood, so it cannot be explained by plasma estrogen levels alone.
span.quote: Interestingly, the sex differences in learning emerge after puberty, whereas no sex differences are observed before or during puberty

span.label: Giving testosterone to newborn females impairs their adult classical conditioning to male-like levels, evidencing an organizational hormone effect.
span.quote: On the other hand, classical conditioning is decremented in adult females if they are treated with testosterone on the day of their birth.

span.label: In conditioned taste aversion acquisition does not differ by sex, but females extinguish the aversion faster, drinking the sweet solution again sooner and in larger amounts.
span.quote: Females typically extinguish sooner than males; they will again consume the sweet solution in less time and do so in greater quantities

span.label: Uncontrollable stress makes male rats fail to escape shock in active avoidance (learned helplessness) while similarly stressed females continue to escape.
span.quote: When male rats are exposed to uncontrollable stress, they do not learn to escape the shock in the active avoidance task and thus they become helpless.

span.label: Because females learn trace eyeblink conditioning better, more of the newly born hippocampal cells survive in females than in males.
span.quote: In a recent study we found that female rats learn better than males in trace eyeblink conditioning and as a consequence a greater proportion of new neurons are rescued in their hippocampus than in males

span.label: Castrating adult males improves their operant avoidance learning, implicating adult testosterone in the male deficit.
span.quote: In contrast, castration of adult males facilitates learning in operant conditioning

span.label: females outperform males in eyeblink conditioning, fear-potentiated startle and most operant tasks
span.quote: In general, females perform better than males in the classical eyeblink conditioning, in fear-potentiated startle and in most operant conditioning tasks, such as the active avoidance test. However, in the classical fear conditioning paradigm, in certain lever-pressing paradigms and in the conditioned taste aversion males outperform females or are more resistant to extinction.

span.label: males outperform females in classical fear conditioning, some lever-pressing tasks and taste aversion
span.quote: In general, females perform better than males in the classical eyeblink conditioning, in fear-potentiated startle and in most operant conditioning tasks, such as the active avoidance test. However, in the classical fear conditioning paradigm, in certain lever-pressing paradigms and in the conditioned taste aversion males outperform females or are more resistant to extinction.

span.label: the direction reverses with task difficulty within lever-pressing
span.quote: Thus, sex differences exist in lever-pressing paradigms with males outperforming females in simple tasks, while females performing better in more difficult tasks, such as the differential reinforcement of low rate responding.

span.label: the eyeblink difference persists in diestrus, so it is not solely an oestrogen effect
span.quote: However, the sex difference is apparent even in females that are trained during diestrus, a phase of the estrous cycle characterized by lower levels of estrogens and progesterone ( Figure 1b ) [ 47 ]. Thus, sex differences are evident across the estrous cycle and are not solely dependent on the presence of estrogens in females.

span.label: females retain the conditioned response better weeks later, which argues the difference is learning and not performance
span.quote: Most convincing is our recent data on memory. In this study, females that are trained and weeks later they are re-exposed to the CS, respond with many more CRs than do males. These data indicate that female rats actually learn the CR better than males and thus they retain it better

span.label: no sex difference exists in spontaneous blinking, in response to the noise alone, or in the unconditioned response
span.quote: In terms of general responsivity, we have never seen any sex difference in spontaneous blinking before training. Neither have we observed any sex differences in eyeblink response to the white noise alone (the eventual CS) before training or in the magnitude of the UR. Also, both males and females do not respond to the first trial, before any US has occurred

span.label: males exposed to uncontrollable stress become helpless while females do not
span.quote: When male rats are exposed to uncontrollable stress, they do not learn to escape the shock in the active avoidance task and thus they become helpless. On the contrary, females exposed to the same regime of uncontrollable stress learn to escape and thus they do not express learned helplessness behaviour

span.label: the helplessness difference survives gonadectomy and neonatal masculinisation, unlike the other effects
span.quote: However, gonadectomy of either sex in adulthood or masculinization of the female brain with testosterone on the day of birth does not prevent sex differences in learned helplessness behaviour

span.label: oestrogen effects on avoidance are non-monotonic - low doses disrupt, high doses facilitate
span.quote: Studies with exogenous estrogens administration showed that low doses of estrogens disrupt, while high doses facilitate acquisition of the active avoidance behaviour

span.label: physiological oestrogen replacement does not restore the eyeblink advantage; only non-physiological doses do
span.quote: On the other hand, estrogens replacement at physiological doses does not enhance conditioning in ovariectomized females. Only very high non-physiological doses of estradiol are effective.

span.label: classical eyeblink conditioning paradigm
span.quote: The classical eyeblink conditioning paradigm is an associative learning task.

span.label: trace conditioning
span.quote: For many of our studies, we rely on a procedure known as trace conditioning. This task depends on the hippocampus and requires multiple trials to learn because the CS is separated with the US with a trace interval of 500 ms.

span.label: delay conditioning
span.quote: Delay conditioning is much easier to learn than trace conditioning, because the CS and the US overlap in time; learning this association does not depend on the hippocampus

span.label: conditioned taste aversion
span.quote: During conditioned taste aversion, animals learn to associate the consumption of a sweet solution with an aversive compound that makes them physically ill.

span.label: fear-potentiated startle paradigm
span.quote: In the fear-potentiated startle paradigm, the rats learn that the presence of a cue, such as a light is paired with a footshock.

span.label: light-enhanced startle paradigm
span.quote: has been used for the development of the light-enhanced startle paradigm, which measures unconditioned anxiety

span.label: one-way avoidance task (FR1)
span.quote: Recently, as part of our learned helplessness studies, we trained male and female rats on the one-way avoidance task (FR1) [ 84 , 85 ]. In this task, the rats must pass through the door way of a shuttle box once, in order to avoid a mild footshock (1 mA)

span.label: two-way avoidance task (FR2)
span.quote: More striking sex differences emerge when males and females are tested on a more difficult task, the two-way avoidance task (FR2) ( Figure 4a ) [ 84 , 85 ]. In this task the rats need to pass twice through the doorway of the shuttle-box, in order to terminate the footshock.

span.label: organizational and activational effects
span.quote: Most sex differences in conditioning are dependent on organizational effects of gonadal hormones during early development of the brain, in addition to modulation by activational effects during puberty and adulthood.

span.label: trace versus delay conditioning
span.quote: For many of our studies, we rely on a procedure known as trace conditioning. This task depends on the hippocampus and requires multiple trials to learn because the CS is separated with the US with a trace interval of 500 ms. We also observe sex differences during delay conditioning. Delay conditioning is much easier to learn than trace conditioning, because the CS and the US overlap in time; learning this association does not depend on the hippocampus

span.label: sex of the rat (intact female vs intact male)
span.term: sex of the rat (intact female vs intact male)
span.quote: b. Intact females emit more conditioned responses than intact males during trace eyeblink conditioning (p<0.05).

span.label: gonadectomy in adulthood (castration of males)
span.quote: c. Castrated adult males learn to escape sooner the mild footshock in the FR2 task, in comparison to gonadally-intact adult males (p<0.05).

span.label: conditioned eyeblink response (EMG of the upper eyelid muscle)
span.term: conditioned eyeblink response (EMG of the upper eyelid muscle)
span.quote: Eyeblinks are detected by an increase in the magnitude of the electromyographical (EMG) response of the muscle of the upper eyelid.

span.label: escape latency in the shuttle box
span.term: escape latency in the shuttle box
span.quote: Gonadally-intact and ovariectomized females exhibit the same escape latencies when they are trained to avoid a mild footshock by passing twice though the doorway of the shuttle box (FR2), for 30 trials in one day

span.label: dendritic spine density on CA1 pyramidal cells
span.term: dendritic spine density on CA1 pyramidal cells
span.quote: Density of dendritic spines is measured in the basal and the apical dendrites of the pyramidal cells.

span.label: stage of the estrous cycle at the start of training
span.term: stage of the estrous cycle at the start of training
span.quote: The magnitude of the sex difference in eyeblink conditioning appears to be sensitive to sex hormone concentrations, because it is most evident when females begin training in proestrus, when estrogens levels are high

span.label: estrous stage held at diestrus on day 1 of training
span.term: estrous stage held at diestrus on day 1 of training
span.quote: In this experiment, all females were in diestrus on the first day of training.

span.label: sex
span.quote: Sex differences have been reported during acquisition, retention and extinction in most of these paradigms. In general, females perform better than males in the classical eyeblink conditioning, in fear-potentiated startle and in most operant conditioning tasks, such as the active avoidance test. However, in the classical fear conditioning paradigm, in certain lever-pressing paradigms and in the conditioned taste aversion males outperform females or are more resistant to extinction.

span.label: phase of the estrous cycle
span.quote: However, the sex difference is apparent even in females that are trained during diestrus, a phase of the estrous cycle characterized by lower levels of estrogens and progesterone ( Figure 1b ) [ 47 ]. Thus, sex differences are evident across the estrous cycle and are not solely dependent on the presence of estrogens in females.

span.label: task difficulty
span.quote: Thus, sex differences exist in lever-pressing paradigms with males outperforming females in simple tasks, while females performing better in more difficult tasks, such as the differential reinforcement of low rate responding.

span.label: 500 ms — length of the temporal gap between CS and US that makes eyeblink conditioning hippocampus-dependent
span.quote: In the hippocampal-dependent task of trace conditioning the two conditioning stimuli are separated by a trace interval or “temporal gap” of 500 ms.

span.label: 800 trials — total trace eyeblink conditioning trials given, spread over four days at 200 per day
span.quote: Rats were trained with 800 trials of trace eyeblink conditioning over a period of 4 days (200 trials/day).

span.label: 34% / 17% — increase in the density of new hippocampal cells caused by training, in females versus males
span.quote: The percent increase is greater in trained females (34%) than in trained males (17%).

span.label: 60% — the responding rate used as the learning criterion that more females than males reach
span.quote: Also, in experiments with a limited number of trials, more females than males reach a learning criterion of 60% responding

span.label: 1 mA — intensity of the footshock the rats learn to avoid in the one-way avoidance task
span.quote: In this task, the rats must pass through the door way of a shuttle box once, in order to avoid a mild footshock (1 mA)

span.label: 30 trials — amount of avoidance training after which some male rats still have not learned to escape
span.quote: In some cases, male rats never learn to escape the shock, even after 30 trials of training

span.label: 500 ms trace interval — the gap that makes the task hippocampus-dependent
span.quote: For many of our studies, we rely on a procedure known as trace conditioning. This task depends on the hippocampus and requires multiple trials to learn because the CS is separated with the US with a trace interval of 500 ms. We also observe sex differences during delay conditioning. Delay conditioning is much easier to learn than trace conditioning, because the CS and the US overlap in time; learning this association does not depend on the hippocampus
